14900:
To sow means to scatter or place seeds in the ground so they can grow into plants. Picture a farmer walking across a field, dropping seeds into the soil — that act is sowing.

But "sow" reaches far beyond farming. In everyday English, it is used to describe starting or spreading anything that will grow or develop over time — ideas, emotions, conflict, doubt. You can sow fear just as a farmer sows wheat.

The single most important thing to understand about this word is: you are beginning something now whose effects will come later. Sowing is always the start of a process, not the end result. The seed goes in the ground today; the plant appears weeks later. The fear is sown today; the panic spreads later.

In its concrete sense, to sow is to put seeds into soil, either by scattering them broadly over an area or by placing them in rows. You can sow seeds in a place, or you can sow a place with seeds — both are correct.

  • "The farmer sowed wheat across the entire field."
  • "She sowed the garden with wildflower seeds."
  • "The hillside was sown with barley."

This is where "sow" becomes truly powerful in English. Just as seeds grow silently underground before they appear, ideas and emotions planted in a person's mind also grow slowly and invisibly. So English uses "sow" to describe starting or spreading something intangible that will develop over time.

What you sow figuratively is almost always an abstract thing:

Sow doubt — to make someone start to question something
"His evasive answers sowed doubt in the jury's mind."

Sow fear — to make people gradually become afraid
"The criminal's threats sowed fear throughout the community."

Sow discord / division — to cause conflict and disagreement to grow between people
"The rumor sowed discord among the teammates."

Sow chaos / confusion — to cause a situation to become disorderly
"The false announcement sowed chaos in the markets."

Sow the seeds of something — to create the early conditions for something to develop later
"Those early conversations sowed the seeds of a lifelong friendship."
"Years of injustice sowed the seeds of revolution."

Notice that in figurative use, "sow" often carries a sense of deliberate intention — someone is doing it on purpose, usually to influence others. And what is sown is often something negative (doubt, fear, conflict), though not always.

Both words can be used with seeds, but they feel different:

  • Plant is more precise and controlled — you place something in one specific spot.
  • Sow suggests spreading more broadly, covering an area.

You plant a tree. You sow a field. You plant a bulb in a hole. You sow grass seed across a whole lawn.

In figurative use, they can sometimes overlap ("plant an idea" / "sow an idea"), but "sow" more strongly implies that the thing will spread and grow over time, the way seeds do across a field.
Grammar: How to Use It in a Sentence

Sow almost always needs an object — you sow something.

PatternExample
Sow + object"She sowed doubt." / "He sowed seeds."
Sow + place + with + object"They sowed the field with corn."
Sow + object + in/into + place"Sow the seeds into well-drained soil."

Tenses:

  • Past tense → sowed ("She sowed the field last spring.")
  • Past participle → sown (preferred) or sowed ("The seeds have been sown." / "Fear was sown into their hearts.")
The Most Famous Phrase: "You Reap What You Sow"

This is one of the most widely used expressions in English, and it perfectly captures the full logic of the word.

To reap means to harvest — to gather the crops that grew from the seeds you planted.

So "you reap what you sow" means: the results you experience in life come directly from your own actions. Your actions are the seeds. The consequences are the harvest. Treat people with kindness → kindness returns to you. Cause harm → harm returns to you.

"He cheated his business partners for years. Now no one trusts him. You reap what you sow."

To "sow wild oats" means to behave in a reckless, irresponsible, or pleasure-seeking way — especially in your youth. The image is that instead of sowing useful crops, you're carelessly scattering wild, unproductive seeds. It often carries a tone of mild disapproval, but sometimes affectionate understanding.

"He spent his twenties sowing wild oats before eventually settling down."

"Sow" is a verb about beginnings that lead to growth. Literally, it means to scatter seeds in the ground. Figuratively, it means to start or spread something — usually something that will develop slowly over time, whether that's doubt, fear, conflict, friendship, or revolution. The word always carries the implication that what you initiate now will grow into something larger later, for better or worse. That is precisely why "you reap what you sow" is such an enduring expression — it captures the full, inevitable cycle: what you begin, you will eventually face.
14901:
When someone is spaced-out, their mind is not fully in the present moment. They feel mentally distant — like they are floating somewhere far away while the world around them continues. Their attention is absent, their thoughts are foggy, and they seem disconnected from what is happening right in front of them.

Think of it this way: imagine an astronaut drifting alone in the vastness of outer space, far from Earth. That image of being remote, detached, and far from the ordinary world is exactly the feeling "spaced-out" captures — except it describes a person's mental state, not a physical location.
The Two Main Senses

"Spaced-out" is used in two closely related ways:

1. Under the influence of drugs

This is the original, most specific sense. Someone who is spaced-out because of drugs (especially marijuana, hallucinogens, or certain medications) appears dazed and detached. Their reactions are slow, their eyes may look glazed or unfocused, they might say things that don't quite make sense, and they are clearly not fully "here." Their mind is elsewhere — in a haze.

"He took one look at her and knew she was completely spaced-out."

2. Dazed, dreamy, or mentally absent — without drugs

This is the broader, everyday sense. A person can be spaced-out simply from exhaustion, boredom, daydreaming, stress, shock, or just being the kind of person whose mind tends to drift. No drugs are involved. They are just... not paying attention to the world around them. Their eyes may be open, they may even be sitting in front of you, but their mind is somewhere else entirely.

"She stared out of the window with that spaced-out look she gets whenever she's tired."

Both senses share the same core: mental absence, haziness, and disconnection from the present.
What It Looks Like (From the Outside)

When you observe a spaced-out person, you typically notice:

  • A blank, faraway stare (sometimes called "staring into space")
  • Slow or delayed responses when you speak to them
  • Confusion about what is going on around them
  • Forgetting what someone just said, or asking you to repeat yourself
  • Moving or speaking slowly and dreamily
  • Giving answers that don't quite fit the question
What It Feels Like (From the Inside)

From the inside, being spaced-out is a soft, fuzzy feeling. Thoughts don't come sharply. The world feels slightly unreal or at a distance, like you are watching it through frosted glass. You might realize vaguely that someone is talking to you, but it takes effort to pull yourself back in. It is not painful or alarming — it is more like being wrapped in a comfortable fog.
Mild vs. Extreme

"Spaced-out" covers a range:

  • Mildly spaced-out: A student who drifts off during a boring lecture and realizes they haven't absorbed the last five minutes. This is very common and harmless.
  • Moderately spaced-out: Someone who is so exhausted after a long international flight that they can't remember where they parked their car or what floor their hotel room is on.
  • Extremely spaced-out: A person under heavy medication or drugs who can barely hold a conversation, keeps losing track of what they were saying, and seems barely aware of their surroundings.
Temporary State vs. Personality Trait

"Spaced-out" can describe either a temporary condition or a characteristic of someone's personality.

  • Temporary: "I'm completely spaced-out today — I barely slept last night." (It will pass once they rest.)
  • Personality trait: "My cousin is such a spaced-out person — she's always forgetting her keys and losing track of conversations." (This is just how she tends to be, generally inattentive and dreamy.)

When describing a personality, "spaced-out" suggests someone who is habitually absent-minded, a bit of a daydreamer, and not very sharp or alert in day-to-day life. It's not harsh or cruel — it's affectionately informal — but it does imply that the person isn't fully switched on.
Tone and Register

"Spaced-out" is informal and colloquial. You would use it in casual conversation, not in a formal essay or a medical report. It has a relaxed, slightly playful quality. It is rarely used with serious negativity — it is more descriptive than judgmental, though it can carry a light teasing quality when used about someone's personality.

It is perfectly acceptable in everyday speech, informal writing, and social contexts.
Situations That Make People Spaced-Out

• Sleep deprivation or extreme tiredness
  • Long travel (especially jet lag)
  • Certain medications (like antihistamines or painkillers)
  • Recreational drugs
  • Deep daydreaming
  • Being overwhelmed or emotionally shocked
  • Hunger or low blood sugar
  • Monotonous, boring tasks that cause the mind to wander
  • Meditation or a very relaxed mental state
Example Sentences

1. "He was so spaced-out after the surgery that he kept calling the nurse by the wrong name."
  2. "Stop being spaced-out and focus — the exam is in ten minutes."
  3. "She had this spaced-out expression on her face, like she was daydreaming about something far away."
  4. "The long train journey left me feeling completely spaced-out and groggy."
  5. "He's always a bit spaced-out — he once showed up to a meeting on the wrong day."
Similar Words and How "Spaced-Out" Compares

Understanding similar words will sharpen your grasp of this one:

  • Absent-minded — similar, but gentler and more about forgetfulness than haziness. An absent-minded person forgets things. A spaced-out person seems generally foggy and disconnected.
  • Dazed — similar, but "dazed" often implies a sudden cause (a shock, a blow to the head, surprising news). "Spaced-out" is softer and can be gradual.
  • Zoned out — nearly identical in meaning; used the same way. "Zoned out" is very common in American English and is essentially a synonym.
  • Dreamy — overlapping, but "dreamy" has a more positive, pleasant, romantic quality. "Spaced-out" is more neutral or slightly negative.
  • Groggy — similar, but "groggy" specifically means physically heavy and sluggish, usually from sleep or illness. "Spaced-out" focuses more on the mental haziness.
  • Out of it — a very close synonym. "He seemed totally out of it" means the same thing as "He seemed totally spaced-out."
A Minor, Less Common Use

In rare cases, "spaced-out" can describe physical objects that are arranged with large or uneven gaps between them — for example, "The chairs were too spaced-out across the room." However, this sense is uncommon and usually written as "spaced out" without a hyphen. When you see "spaced-out" as a hyphenated adjective describing a person, it almost always means the mental state described above.
In Summary

Spaced-out means mentally foggy, absent, and disconnected from the present moment — whether from drugs, tiredness, daydreaming, or just a naturally drifting mind. The person is physically present but mentally somewhere far away, responding slowly, thinking hazily, and not fully engaged with what is happening around them. It is a casual, informal word, used warmly and descriptively in everyday speech.
14902:
Spacious means having a lot of space — large, open, and roomy, with plenty of room to move around, breathe, or fit things in comfortably.

When you call something spacious, you're saying it doesn't feel tight, crowded, or cramped. There is generous, comfortable room.
What It Describes

Spacious is almost always used to describe enclosed or bounded places — physical areas that have a size or boundary. Think:

  • Rooms, apartments, houses, halls
  • Car interiors, cabins, offices
  • Gardens, terraces, lawns
  • Closets, kitchens, living areas

"They moved into a spacious three-bedroom apartment."
"The hotel lobby was spacious and elegantly decorated."
"She loved her spacious office with its large windows."
What Makes a Place "Spacious"

A place feels spacious when it has:

  • Wide, open floor area — plenty of room to walk around freely
  • High ceilings — these make a room feel tall and open
  • Little clutter or overcrowding — not too much furniture crammed in
  • A general sense of openness and freedom of movement

It's not just about raw size in metres or square feet — it's about how generous and uncongested the space feels.
The Positive Feeling Built Into the Word

Here's something important: "spacious" is always a positive word. When you say a room is spacious, you're giving it a compliment. It suggests comfort, freedom, and even a touch of luxury.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "The room is big." — neutral, just states a fact
  • "The room is spacious." — warm and positive, implies the size is a pleasure

This is why the word appears so often in real estate advertisements and hotel descriptions — sellers use it because it makes you feel good about a property.
How Strong Is It?

"Spacious" implies generously large — more than just "enough." It doesn't mean the place is enormous or overwhelming in size, but it does mean the size is noticeably comfortable and beyond what feels tight.

Think of it on a scale:
cramped → small → adequate → roomy → spacious → vast

"Spacious" sits at the comfortable, generous end without going to the extreme of "vast" (which suggests something almost overwhelming in size).
Common Sentence Patterns

Spacious is a standard describing adjective and fits naturally in these patterns:

  • Before a noun: a spacious kitchen, a spacious car, a spacious park
  • After "is/feels/looks/seems": The apartment feels spacious. / The hall looks spacious.

"After years in a tiny studio, their new home felt wonderfully spacious."
"The cabin was surprisingly spacious for a mountain retreat."
"Removing the wall made the living room far more spacious."
Synonyms — and How They Differ

These words are close in meaning, but each has its own shade:

  • Roomy — informal, friendly, almost identical to spacious; "a roomy car"
  • Ample — means more than enough; emphasises sufficiency more than openness; "ample storage"
  • Capacious — more formal; focuses on how much something can hold or contain; "a capacious bag"
  • Expansive — emphasises something spreading widely outward, often used for outdoor or landscape views; "an expansive garden"
  • Airy — overlaps with spacious but leans more into light and ventilation than pure size; "a bright, airy room"
  • Vast — much stronger; suggests an almost overwhelming, enormous scale; not used for ordinary rooms

Among all these, spacious is the most balanced and widely used for describing indoor and human-scale environments in a warm, pleasing way.
Antonyms — The Opposites

• Cramped — the direct opposite; uncomfortably small and tight; "a cramped office"
  • Confined — restricted, closed-in feeling
  • Narrow — specifically limited in width
  • Cluttered — not technically about size, but a cluttered space loses its feeling of spaciousness
  • Poky (British English) — informal word for a small, cramped space

A spacious room has room to breathe. A cramped room makes you feel squeezed.
A Subtle Metaphorical Use

Occasionally, "spacious" is used in a non-physical, figurative sense to describe thinking, writing, or the mind — suggesting something open, unrushed, and broad rather than narrow or rigid.

"His writing has a spacious quality — it doesn't rush you."
"She approached problems with a spacious, unhurried mind."

This use is less common but perfectly natural in literary or thoughtful contexts.
Register and Tone

"Spacious" is a standard English word — not too formal, not slangy. It fits naturally in:

  • Everyday conversation
  • Writing and descriptions
  • Real estate, travel, interior design language
  • Literature and journalism

You can use it comfortably in any situation without it sounding out of place.
The One-Line Summary
Spacious means generously large and open, with plenty of comfortable room — and it always carries a positive, pleasant feeling.
14903:
Span means the full reach or extent from one end to the other — like measuring "how far" or "how long" something stretches, whether in space or in time.

Think of it this way: if you spread your hand wide open, the distance from the tip of your thumb to the tip of your little finger is a "span." That image — something stretching fully from one side to the other — is what this word is always doing, in every situation.

1. A Distance — From One Side to the Other

This is the most physical, visual meaning of span. It refers to the length of something measured across its full width.

A bridge's span is the distance from one end of the bridge to the other (or between its two supporting pillars). A bird's wingspan is the span of its wings from tip to tip. A rainbow has a span — the full arc it stretches across the sky.

The key feel here is that you're measuring something that connects two points or reaches all the way across something.

Examples:

  • "The span of the new bridge is 400 meters."
  • "She measured the span of the doorway before buying the curtain rod."
  • "The eagle has a span of nearly two meters."

2. A Length of Time — A Period or Duration

Just as span can measure physical distance, it can also measure how long something lasts in time. Here, it means a stretch of time — from a beginning point to an end point.

This is probably the most common use you will encounter in everyday life.

Examples:

  • "He finished the entire book in a span of two days."
  • "A lot changed over a span of ten years."
  • "Try to focus for a span of 30 minutes without distractions."

Notice the structure: "a span of [amount of time]" — this phrasing is very natural in English.

3. The Full Range or Extent of Something

Span can also describe the total scope of something — how far it reaches across a subject, a space, or a scale. This is a broader, more abstract use.

Examples:

  • "His knowledge spans — his span of knowledge — covered art, science, and philosophy."
  • "The damage was visible across the entire span of the building's east wall."
  • "This museum holds works that cover the full span of human history."

Here, span isn't so much about measuring a specific number but about expressing totality — the wholeness of how far something goes.

4. A Unit of Measurement (Informal/Old-fashioned)

In older and sometimes informal use, a span is a rough unit of length equal to the spread of a human hand — from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger — roughly 9 inches or about 23 centimeters. You are less likely to encounter this in modern daily English, but you may find it in older books, the Bible, or traditional literature.

Example:

  • "He measured the cloth — it was roughly three spans wide."

5. Engineering / Architecture — The Clear Distance Between Supports

In construction and architecture, span has a very precise and important meaning: the horizontal distance between two structural supports, such as the pillars of a bridge, the walls of a room, or the columns of an arch.

This is essentially an extension of the first meaning (distance across), but applied technically.

Examples:

  • "The arch has a span of 60 feet."
  • "Engineers had to calculate the span carefully before designing the roof."

These are common combinations where "span" appears as a noun:

Attention span — how long a person can concentrate without losing focus.
"Young children typically have a short attention span."

Life span / lifespan — the length of time a living creature lives, or a product or thing is expected to function.
"The average lifespan of a sea turtle is over 80 years."
"The lifespan of this battery is about 5 years."

Time span — simply another way of saying "a period of time." Very common.
"All of this happened within a remarkably short time span."

A span of time — the most natural way to say "a period of time" with this word.
"We haven't spoken in a span of about three months."

In the span of — meaning "within the time of" or "over a period of."
"In the span of a single year, she learned two new languages."

Once you see the common thread, the word becomes easy to remember. Every single meaning of span comes back to the same instinct: the distance between two endpoints — whether those endpoints are physical (two sides of a bridge), temporal (the beginning and end of a period), or abstract (the full extent of something's reach).

Span always asks the same silent question: "From where to where? From when to when? How far does this go?"

SituationWhat "span" means

If you are talking about space, span is the distance across something. If you are talking about time, span is how long a period lasts. If you are talking about knowledge, damage, a career, or any broad subject, span is how wide or far it reaches. In all cases, the word carries the same energy: full stretch, from one end to the other.
14904:
To span means to stretch across something from one end to the other, covering everything in between.

Think of a bridge over a river. The bridge doesn't just touch one bank — it reaches all the way across to the other side, covering the full gap. That is exactly what "span" means: complete coverage from point A to point B, with nothing left out in the middle.

This one idea — reaching fully across something — is what drives every use of this word.
The Three Main Ways It Is Used

1. Physical Space

When something physically stretches across a distance, it spans that distance.

  • The bridge spans the river.
  • Her arms couldn't span the width of the enormous table.
  • A single cable spans the entire length of the ceiling.

Here, "span" is almost a synonym for "cross" or "stretch across," but with the added sense that the full gap is covered — not just crossed at one point.

2. Time

This is perhaps the most common modern use. When something spans a period of time, it lasts through that entire period — from start to finish.

  • Her career spanned forty years. (It lasted from one point all the way to another, forty years later.)
  • The war spanned nearly a decade.
  • The novel spans three generations of one family.

Notice the key idea again: the career didn't just touch the beginning and the end of forty years. It covered all forty years. That sense of completeness — covering the full stretch — is always present.

3. Abstract Range or Scope

"Span" is also used when something covers a wide range of subjects, fields, places, or categories — even when there is no physical distance or clock time involved.

  • His knowledge spans many different fields, from science to art.
  • The company's influence spans six continents.
  • The exhibition spans a huge variety of artistic styles.

Again, the idea is full, unbroken coverage across a range — not just touching a few points here and there.
The Important Nuance: It Implies Completeness

This is the sharpest and most important thing to understand about "span."

When you say something spans something, you are saying it covers the whole thing — start to finish, side to side, with nothing skipped. It is not a word for partial coverage.

Compare:

  • Her career touched on many areas of music. → She dipped into various areas.
  • Her career spanned many areas of music. → She covered the full breadth of them.

The second sentence is stronger and implies a sense of full, unbroken reach.

FormExample
Base formto span
Present (he/she/it)The bridge spans the valley.
Past tenseHer rule spanned twenty years.
Past participleA period spanned by great change.
Present participlea career-spanning collection of songs

Picture a hand stretching out flat across a surface — fingertip to fingertip, covering everything underneath. That image of reaching fully from one side to the other, leaving no gap, is exactly what "to span" means, whether it applies to a river, a century, or a field of knowledge.

To span = to extend fully from one end to another, covering the complete distance, time, or range in between. It can describe physical space, periods of time, or abstract ranges of topics, subjects, or influence. The defining quality of the word is completeness — whatever is spanned is covered in its entirety.
14905: A spangle is a small, thin, flat, shiny disc or piece of glittering material. Its defining quality is that it catches light and throws it back brilliantly, creating a sparkling, eye-catching effect. Think of the tiny, circular, glittery decorations you see sewn all over a dancer's costume or a glamorous party dress — those are spangles.

A spangle is very small — typically no bigger than a fingernail, often much smaller. It is flat, not three-dimensional. It is made of metal, or a metallic material, so its surface is shiny and reflective. When light hits a spangle at any angle, it bounces off and glitters. When hundreds of spangles are sewn closely together on a piece of fabric, the whole surface seems to shimmer and sparkle as the wearer moves.

Spangles appear most commonly on clothing and costumes that are meant to dazzle — circus performer outfits, ballroom dancing costumes, stage and theatre costumes, cheerleading uniforms, and glamorous evening gowns. The purpose is always decoration and visual brilliance: a garment covered in spangles is impossible to ignore under a spotlight.

You may already know the word "sequin." A sequin and a spangle refer to essentially the same object — a small, shiny, flat disc used as a decorative ornament on clothing. "Sequin" is the more modern and widely used term, while "spangle" is older and somewhat more literary or formal in feel, but they describe the same thing. If you can picture a sequined dress, you can picture a spangled one.

Beyond the literal physical object, "spangle" is also used figuratively to describe any small, bright, sparkling point of light — something that glitters the way a real spangle does. In this sense, stars in the night sky are often called spangles in poetry and descriptive writing, because they appear as tiny, brilliant points of light scattered across a dark background, just like glittery discs scattered across dark fabric.

This figurative sense is exactly where the phrase "Star-Spangled Banner" — the title of the American national anthem and a name for the American flag — comes from. The flag is "star-spangled," meaning it is covered with stars that glitter like spangles. The stars on the flag act as the spangles; the flag is the fabric they are scattered across.

"Her costume was covered from top to bottom in silver spangles, and she blazed like a mirror ball under the stage lights."

"Looking up at the clear night sky, he saw thousands of spangles scattered across the darkness."

"The old ballroom gown had lost several of its golden spangles, leaving small bare patches on the bodice."
The single idea to hold onto

Whether used literally or figuratively, a spangle always means the same fundamental thing: something small, flat, shiny, and brilliantly glittering — a tiny concentrated point of sparkle. The word carries a sense of glamour, decoration, and light. Wherever there is deliberate, decorative shimmer — on a costume, in the sky, on a surface — the word "spangle" fits perfectly.
14906: A spaniel is a type of dog — not a single specific breed, but a whole group of dog breeds that share certain physical features and personality traits. Think of it like how "terrier" or "hound" refers to a family of related dogs. A spaniel is one such family.

Spaniels are easy to recognize once you know what to look for. They tend to be small to medium-sized dogs with:

  • Long, floppy ears that hang down on the sides of their face — this is probably their most recognizable feature.
  • Soft, wavy or silky fur, often with longer, feathery hair on their ears, chest, legs, and tail.
  • Large, round, soulful eyes that give them a gentle, almost melting expression — the kind of look that makes people feel immediately warm toward them.
  • A sturdy but graceful body, built for movement through fields, water, and undergrowth.
What spaniels are like in personality

Spaniels are known for being affectionate, eager to please, loyal, and lively. They love being around people and are generally very friendly — with their owners, with strangers, and often with other animals too. They are energetic and enjoy exercise, but they are also happy to curl up close to a person they love.

Because of these traits, spaniels are considered excellent companion dogs and family pets. They are sensitive animals — they respond well to kindness and can become anxious or withdrawn if treated harshly.
What spaniels were originally bred to do

Spaniels were originally working dogs, bred centuries ago to help hunters. Their job had two main parts:

  1. Flushing — running through dense undergrowth, bushes, or tall grass to disturb and drive out birds (like pheasants or woodcock) hiding there, so the hunter could shoot them.
  2. Retrieving — fetching the shot birds and bringing them back to the hunter, often from water, since many spaniels are strong swimmers.

This hunting background explains why spaniels are energetic, have a keen nose, and love to explore their surroundings. Even pet spaniels today often show instincts like sniffing everything thoroughly or darting after birds.

Since "spaniel" is a group, there are many individual breeds within it. Some of the most well-known are:

  • Cocker Spaniel — one of the most popular and well-loved, known for its sweet temperament and silky coat. There are two varieties: the English Cocker Spaniel and the American Cocker Spaniel (slightly smaller, with a rounder head and more abundant fur).
  • Cavalier King Charles Spaniel — a very small, gentle, and deeply affectionate breed, often considered among the most loving of all dog breeds. Historically a lapdog of royalty.
  • English Springer Spaniel — larger and more athletic than a Cocker Spaniel, with great energy and a strong instinct for fieldwork.
  • Field Spaniel, Clumber Spaniel, Sussex Spaniel, Welsh Springer Spaniel — less common varieties, each with their own distinct look and character, but all part of the same family.

Despite their differences in size and appearance, all these breeds share the essential "spaniel" traits: the ears, the coat, the temperament, and the working instinct.

Today, most spaniels are kept as companion animals rather than hunting dogs. They fit well into family life because they are gentle with children, sociable, and not aggressive. However, they do need regular exercise and mental stimulation — a bored spaniel can become anxious or destructive. Their long ears and silky coats also require regular cleaning and grooming to stay healthy.
The figurative use of the word

Outside of its literal meaning, "spaniel" is sometimes used figuratively in English — usually in literature or formal writing — to describe a person who is excessively servile or fawning: someone who follows another person around eagerly, trying to please them at every turn, almost embarrassingly so.

This usage draws directly from the dog's nature. A spaniel is devoted and eager to please its master. So calling a person a "spaniel" (or saying they behave like one) suggests they are overly submissive, lacking in dignity, and desperate for approval or favor from someone more powerful. This figurative sense carries a mildly contemptuous tone — it implies the person has surrendered their own self-respect.

This metaphorical use appears in Shakespeare and other classic literature, so you may encounter it in older texts.

A spaniel is a group of dog breeds characterized by long floppy ears, a soft silky coat, and a gentle, loyal, eager-to-please nature — originally bred as hunting dogs, now mostly beloved as companion animals — and the word can also be used figuratively to describe a person who is obsequiously devoted to another.
14907:
To spar means to engage in a fight or argument with someone — but in a controlled, non-deadly, back-and-forth way. It is not a real, all-out fight. It is more like a practiced, skilled exchange — whether of fists or words — where both sides are actively pushing against each other, but nobody is trying to truly destroy the other.

Think of it as the difference between a war and a friendly wrestling match in the backyard. A war is a real fight. The backyard match is sparring.
Meaning 1: Physical Sparring (Boxing and Martial Arts)

This is the original and most literal meaning.

When two boxers or martial artists spar, they practice fighting techniques on each other. They throw punches, dodge, block, and move — but it is a training exercise, not a real match. The goal is to sharpen your skills, not to knock your partner unconscious.

"The boxer spars with his trainer every morning before a big fight."

Key things to notice here:

  • It is practice, not a real contest.
  • Both people are willing participants — no one is being ambushed.
  • There is skill involved — it is not random swinging.
  • It is repeated — fighters spar regularly, not just once.

This is the figurative meaning, and it is used extremely often in everyday English.

When two people spar with words, they exchange sharp disagreements, witty comebacks, or opposing arguments in a lively, back-and-forth way. Just like physical sparring, it implies:

  • Both people are actively engaged — it's not one person lecturing while the other stays silent.
  • Neither side is trying to completely destroy the other — there's a certain amount of sport or play to it.
  • It often suggests the two people are evenly matched — sharp, intelligent, and capable.

"The two politicians have been sparring over the new tax policy for weeks."
"She and her brother love to spar about football — it goes on for hours."
"The lawyer and the judge sparred throughout the entire hearing."

Notice how in all these examples, the conflict is real — there is genuine disagreement — but it has a controlled, energetic, almost rhythmic quality to it. Nobody is storming off or destroying a relationship. They're pushing against each other with skill.
The Soul of the Word: What Makes "Spar" Unique

This is what separates spar from simple words like fight or argue:

1. It implies repetition and an ongoing relationship.
You don't spar with a stranger once and never again. Sparring partners do it regularly. When you say two people "spar," it suggests this is a recurring dynamic between them.

2. It implies some level of control or mutual willingness.
A mugging is not sparring. A screaming match where someone breaks down in tears is not sparring. Sparring has an almost athletic quality — both sides are in it, both sides are capable, and it doesn't spiral out of control.

3. It implies skill and intelligence.
You don't spar clumsily. The word carries a subtle compliment — to describe someone as a good sparring partner means they are sharp, challenging, and engaging.

4. The fight is never truly finished.
In a real fight, there is usually a winner and a loser. In sparring, the exchange ends and picks up again another day. It is a continuous back-and-forth, not a final resolution.

A sparring partner is the person you regularly spar with — physically or verbally. In boxing, it literally means the training partner you practice fights with. In everyday life, it refers to someone you habitually debate or argue with, often with affection or respect.

"My college roommate was my intellectual sparring partner — we debated everything from politics to philosophy."

This phrase is widely used and very natural in English.

WordHow it differs from "spar"
FightMore serious, more real, more damaging. A fight can be ugly and final. Sparring is controlled.
ArgueMore neutral and straightforward. "Argue" doesn't carry the sense of skill, playfulness, or ongoing rhythm that "spar" does.
DebateMore formal and structured. Sparring is more dynamic, spontaneous, and combative.
BanterPurely playful and friendly. Sparring can have genuine edge and real disagreement behind it.

To spar = to fight or argue with someone in a skilled, controlled, back-and-forth way — not to truly destroy them, but to actively push against them, repeatedly, as a kind of practiced, energetic contest.

It lives in the space between a friendly chat and an all-out war. It is combative but not catastrophic. It is serious but not fatal. And it is almost always between two people who are well-matched and will be back at it again tomorrow.
14908: Before diving in, here is a single idea that sits at the heart of nearly every meaning of spare: the absence of excess. Nothing wasted. Nothing more than what is needed. Keep this in mind and the different meanings will feel like natural variations of one idea, not a confusing jumble.
Meaning 1 — Extra, held in reserve, not currently being used

This is the most common, everyday meaning. A spare thing is something you have in addition to what you are already using. It sits quietly in the background, doing nothing, waiting for the moment it is needed.

Think of a spare key. You have one key you use every day. Your spare key lives in a drawer — until the day you lock yourself out. That is the moment the spare key steps in.

A spare room is a bedroom in your house that nobody regularly sleeps in — it's available for guests. A spare tire lives in the trunk of your car and is only pulled out when one of your four tires gets a flat. Spare parts are extra components stored in a warehouse so that when a machine breaks, a replacement piece is ready. Spare time is time not taken up by work or duties — your free, uncommitted hours. Spare change is the small coins left over in your pocket with no immediate purpose.

The key idea: the spare thing is not currently deployed. It is available, waiting, standing by. That is what makes it spare and not merely "extra" — it has a specific future role, should it ever be called upon.
Meaning 2 — Lean, thin, carrying no excess on the body

When spare describes a person's physical build, it means lean — a body with little excess weight, perhaps showing angles and edges, taut rather than rounded. Crucially, it is a dignified, even admiring word. It does not suggest weakness or illness the way skinny sometimes can.

"He was a spare, weathered man who looked like he'd spent decades doing hard physical work." Here, spare suggests a body that has been stripped down to muscle and purpose, with nothing extra. "She had a spare, athletic frame" paints the picture of someone lean and capable.

This meaning appears more in literary and formal writing than in casual conversation. If you call someone spare in their build, you are implying a kind of deliberate, almost sculptural leanness — a body that has nothing on it that does not belong.
Meaning 3 — Plain, simple, with nothing unnecessary

This is perhaps the richest meaning. When spare describes a style — in writing, art, architecture, speech, or design — it means deliberately minimal. Every element has a purpose. Nothing has been added for decoration or show. Nothing is wasted.

Hemingway's writing is famously described as spare. His sentences are short, direct, and stripped of ornament. There are no extra adjectives piled on, no flourishes, no sentences that exist just to sound beautiful. Each word earns its place, or it is cut.

"The apartment had a spare, elegant design" calls to mind clean lines, empty surfaces, and a sense of calm — nothing cluttered, nothing decorative for its own sake. "She had a spare way of speaking" means she chose her words carefully, said exactly what she meant, and did not ramble.

There is quiet admiration baked into this meaning. A spare style is seen as disciplined and confident, because it takes more skill to say something powerfully with few words than to bury it in many. In a spare work, every element is exposed — there is nowhere to hide.

This meaning is older and less common in everyday modern speech, but you will encounter it in literature and formal writing. A spare meal or spare diet means simple and plain, perhaps barely sufficient — not rich, not generous, not lavish.

"The soldiers survived on a spare diet of bread and dried meat." "They led a spare existence, with few comforts." Here, spare carries a tinge of austerity or hardship — a life or meal stripped down to essentials, with little abundance. It is not quite the same as saying something is "small" — it implies a kind of deliberate or imposed simplicity, a life lived at the minimum.
How to tell the meanings apart at a glance

The context almost always tells you which meaning applies. If someone is talking about a key, a room, a tire, or time → it is the "extra, in reserve" meaning. If the word is describing a person's body → it is "lean and thin." If it is describing a style of writing, art, or design → it is "minimal and unornamented." If it is describing a diet, rations, or a way of living → it is "meager and plain."

Now step back. Look at all four meanings together.

A spare key is the one not being used — beyond the current need, held back. A spare figure has no excess body fat — nothing beyond what the body requires. A spare prose style has no excess words — nothing beyond what the writing needs. A spare diet has no excess richness — barely beyond the minimum.

In every case, spare quietly points to the same truth: this thing — this body, this style, this meal, this object — does not overdo. It is exactly what it needs to be, and nothing more. That restraint is the soul of the word.
14909: "Spare" as a verb always revolves around one idea: holding back, or choosing not to use something fully. That "something" can be your power to hurt someone, an unpleasant experience, or a resource you own. From that one core idea, three distinct meanings grow.
Meaning 1: To Choose Not to Harm, Punish, or Kill

When you have the power to hurt someone — and you deliberately choose not to — you spare them.

Examples:

  • "The king spared the prisoner's life." → He could have ordered the execution, but he didn't.
  • "Please spare me — I meant no harm." → A plea: "Don't punish me."
  • "The hurricane spared the coastal villages." → The storm had the destructive power, but those villages escaped damage.

The key idea: There is a real threat or power on one side, and a conscious decision on the other side to not use it. This is why "spare" in this sense carries a strong emotional weight — someone is being shown mercy.
Meaning 2: To Protect Someone From an Unpleasant Experience

Here, you don't spare someone from harm you would cause — instead, you prevent them from going through something uncomfortable or unnecessary.

The structure is usually: spare + someone + something

Examples:

  • "Spare me the details." → Don't make me sit through the unpleasant or boring details; protect me from them.
  • "I'll spare you the trouble." → I'll handle it so you don't have to go through the effort or difficulty.
  • "The good news spared her a lot of worry." → Because of the good news, she didn't have to suffer through anxiety.

The key idea: You are acting as a shield. You step between a person and something unpleasant so they don't have to face it.

How this differs from Meaning 1:
In Meaning 1, you are the source of the potential harm, and you hold back.
In Meaning 2, the unpleasant thing comes from elsewhere, and you protect the person from it.
Meaning 3: To Give or Make Something Available From What You Have

When you have a resource — time, money, attention, energy — and you can afford to offer some of it without seriously running short yourself, you spare it.

Examples:

  • "Can you spare a few minutes?" → Do you have some extra minutes you can give me?
  • "I can't spare the money right now." → I have no money left over to give; I need it all.
  • "She couldn't spare a single soldier for the mission." → Every soldier was already needed elsewhere; none could be released.
  • "Do you have a pen to spare?" → Do you have an extra one you can give away?

The key idea: "Spare" here always implies you have a supply of something, and you're giving from what's left over or extra. If you say you can't spare something, it means your supply is too tight — you need all of it yourself.

You'll often see "spare" used in the phrase "spare no expense / spare no effort / spare no resource."

  • "They spared no expense on the wedding." → They held nothing back; they spent as much money as it took.
  • "She spared no effort to make him comfortable." → She gave everything she had; she didn't hold back any effort.

This is the negative of Meaning 3. Instead of keeping something back, you release all of it — you use everything.

Think of "spare" as the verb of restraint and release. You are always deciding whether to use something fully or hold it back:

SituationWhat you're holding back
Meaning 1Your power to harm
Meaning 2An unpleasant experience (from reaching someone)
Meaning 3A resource (you release some of it, or you hold it back)
A Few Final Notes on Usage

"Spare me" is also used informally and sarcastically to mean "Don't bother saying that — I don't want to hear it."

  • "Oh, spare me the excuses." → I don't want to hear your justifications.

"If you can spare it" is a polite, considerate way of asking for something — it shows you're aware the other person might not have extra.

  • "Could you lend me your umbrella, if you can spare it?"

"Spare yourself" means to protect yourself from unnecessary trouble or pain.

  • "Spare yourself the stress — just book the ticket early."

Once you understand that "spare" is fundamentally about not using something fully — whether that's your power, a bad experience, or a resource — all its uses fall into place naturally.
